counterfactual_missing_items: There were no signs of steroid-induced atrophy, such as skin thinning or increased vascular prominence
She denied fever, systemic symptoms, or personal or family history of atopy
A few pustules were also noted in the perioral area
decisive_items: She had been applying this ointment to her face at least daily for 2 years, pausing for no more than 1–2 days at a time because the rash promptly returned
She stopped the ointment completely 3 days before presentation.
There were confluent erythematous, edematous plaques in the bilateral periorbital areas (left more than right), studded with numerous 2– to 3-mm pustules, some coalescing into “lakes of pus.”
response.rationale: R1 uniquely integrates the 2-year daily topical corticosteroid exposure, abrupt cessation, and the periorificial pustular/edematous eruption, making steroid-induced rosacea-like dermatitis the most complete diagnosis. R4 captures the morphology and distribution but omits the steroid-induced cause; R3 addresses only withdrawal; R2 lacks any contact allergen or temporal contact exposure.

rejected.why: Only the cessation span is cited; it does not account for the 2-year daily steroid exposure or the pustular periorificial morphology.
No contact allergen or temporal contact exposure is present; the eruption follows steroid withdrawal, not a contactant.
